claim: Metformin inhibits mitochondrial complex I (NADH dehydrogenase) activity in human cancer cells.
source: In this study, we report that in human cancer cells, metformin inhibits mitochondrial complex I (NADH dehydrogenase) activity and cellular respiration.
evidence: The abstract directly states this finding, which is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Metformin inhibits cellular respiration in human cancer cells.
source: In this study, we report that in human cancer cells, metformin inhibits mitochondrial complex I (NADH dehydrogenase) activity and cellular respiration.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, supported by oxygen consumption measurements in Figure 1.

claim: Metformin inhibited cellular proliferation in the presence of glucose.
source: Metformin inhibited cellular proliferation in the presence of glucose, but induced cell death upon glucose deprivation, indicating that cancer cells rely exclusively on glycolysis for survival in the presence of metformin.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, supported by cell proliferation data in Figure 2E,F.

claim: Metformin induced cell death upon glucose deprivation.
source: Metformin inhibited cellular proliferation in the presence of glucose, but induced cell death upon glucose deprivation, indicating that cancer cells rely exclusively on glycolysis for survival in the presence of metformin.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, supported by cell viability data in Figure 2C,D.

claim: Cancer cells rely exclusively on glycolysis for survival in the presence of metformin.
source: Metformin inhibited cellular proliferation in the presence of glucose, but induced cell death upon glucose deprivation, indicating that cancer cells rely exclusively on glycolysis for survival in the presence of metformin.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that metformin causes cell death when glucose is removed but not when glucose is present.

claim: Metformin reduced hypoxic activation of hypoxia-inducible factor 1 (HIF-1).
source: Metformin also reduced hypoxic activation of hypoxia-inducible factor 1 (HIF-1).
evidence: The abstract states this finding, supported by Western blot and gene expression data in Figure 6.

claim: All effects of metformin were reversed when the metformin-resistant Saccharomyces cerevisiae NADH dehydrogenase NDI1 was overexpressed.
source: All of these effects of metformin were reversed when the metformin-resistant Saccharomyces cerevisiae NADH dehydrogenase NDI1 was overexpressed.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, supported by data throughout the manuscript showing NDI1-expressing cells are resistant to metformin effects.

claim: Administration of metformin to mice inhibited the growth of control human cancer cells but not those expressing NDI1.
source: In vivo, the administration of metformin to mice inhibited the growth of control human cancer cells but not those expressing NDI1.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, supported by xenograft tumor growth data in Figure 7.

claim: Metformin's inhibitory effects on cancer progression are cancer cell autonomous.
source: Thus, we have demonstrated that metformin's inhibitory effects on cancer progression are cancer cell autonomous and depend on its ability to inhibit mitochondrial complex I.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the in vivo experiments showing NDI1-expressing tumors are resistant to metformin.

claim: Metformin's inhibitory effects on cancer progression depend on its ability to inhibit mitochondrial complex I.
source: Thus, we have demonstrated that metformin's inhibitory effects on cancer progression are cancer cell autonomous and depend on its ability to inhibit mitochondrial complex I.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the genetic rescue experiments with NDI1 throughout the manuscript.

claim: Metformin is widely used to treat patients with type II diabetes mellitus who have high levels of circulating insulin.
source: Metformin is widely used to treat patients with type II diabetes mellitus who have high levels of circulating insulin (Nathan et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established medical literature.

claim: Metformin suppresses liver gluconeogenesis thereby reducing glucose release from the liver.
source: Metformin suppresses liver gluconeogenesis thereby reducing glucose release from the liver (Inzucchi et al., 1998; Viollet et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: There is an association between metformin use and diminished tumor progression in patients suffering from different types of cancers.
source: In several recent retrospective studies, investigators have observed an association between metformin use and diminished tumor progression in patients suffering from different types of cancers (Evans et al., 2005; Bowker et al., 2006; Dowling et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to epidemiological studies.

claim: The underlying mechanism by which metformin diminishes tumor growth is not fully understood.
source: However, the underlying mechanism by which metformin diminishes tumor growth is not fully understood.
evidence: This statement establishes the knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: Metformin may act at the organismal level, reducing levels of circulating insulin, a known mitogen for cancer cells.
source: Metformin may act at the organismal level, reducing levels of circulating insulin, a known mitogen for cancer cells.
evidence: This is presented as one of two postulated mechanisms.

claim: Metformin is known to inhibit mitochondrial complex I in vitro.
source: Metformin is known to inhibit mitochondrial complex I in vitro (Ota et al., 2009; El-Mir et al., 2000; Owen et al., 2000)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Cancer cells have the ability to survive on ATP produced exclusively by glycolysis.
source: This latter hypothesis has been questioned as cancer cells have the ability to survive on ATP produced exclusively by glycolysis.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about cancer cell metabolism.

claim: Cancer cells have been shown to conduct glutamine-dependent reductive carboxylation to generate the TCA cycle intermediates required for cell proliferation when the electron transport chain is inhibited.
source: Furthermore, cancer cells have been shown to conduct glutamine-dependent reductive carboxylation to generate the TCA cycle intermediates required for cell proliferation when the electron transport chain is inhibited (Mullen et al., 2012; Fendt et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Human HCT116 p53−/− colon cancer cells have previously shown to be sensitive to metformin.
source: Human HCT116 p53−/− colon cancer cells have previously shown to be sensitive to metformin (Buzzai et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Metformin inhibited cellular oxygen consumption of HCT 116 p53−/− cells at concentrations (0.25–1.0 mM) similar to those reported to affect bioenergetics and gluconeogenesis in primary hepatocytes in vitro.
source: Metformin inhibited cellular oxygen consumption of HCT 116 p53−/− cells at concentrations (0.25–1.0 mM) similar to those reported to affect bioenergetics and gluconeogenesis in primary hepatocytes in vitro (Figure 1A; Foretz et al., 2010; Miller et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1A and citations to prior research.

claim: NDI1 is a single-subunit NADH dehydrogenase, which oxidizes NADH in a process similar to the multi-subunit mammalian complex I; however without proton pumping or ROS generation.
source: NDI1 is a single-subunit NADH dehydrogenase, which oxidizes NADH in a process similar to the multi-subunit mammalian complex I; however without proton pumping or ROS generation (Seo et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research characterizing NDI1.

claim: Mammalian complex I contains 45 subunits that pumps protons and generates ROS.
source: By contrast, mammalian complex I contains 45 subunits that pumps protons and generates ROS.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about mammalian complex I.

claim: NDI1-HCT 116 p53−/− cells were completely resistant to the effects of metformin on cellular oxygen consumption.
source: NDI1-HCT 116 p53−/− cells demonstrated a slight, non-significant elevation in basal cellular oxygen consumption compared to control cells and were completely resistant to the effects of metformin on cellular oxygen consumption (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Saponin removes cholesterol from plasma membranes, allowing the entry of metabolic substrates directly to mitochondria.
source: Saponin removes cholesterol from plasma membranes, allowing the entry of metabolic substrates directly to mitochondria (Jamur and Oliver, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: In the presence of ADP and the complex I substrates pyruvate and malate, metformin fully inhibited oxygen consumption in permeabilized Control-HCT 116 p53−/− cells.
source: In the presence of ADP and the complex I substrates pyruvate and malate, metformin fully inhibited oxygen consumption in permeabilized Control-HCT 116 p53−/− cells (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1C.

claim: Metformin had no effect on pyruvate/malate-driven oxygen consumption in NDI1-HCT 116 p53−/− cells.
source: By contrast, metformin had no effect on pyruvate/malate-driven oxygen consumption in NDI1-HCT 116 p53−/− cells (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1D.

claim: Metformin had no effect on oxygen consumption in saponin-permeabilized cells respiring on the complex II substrate succinate in the presence of ADP.
source: Metformin also had no effect on oxygen consumption in saponin-permeabilized cells respiring on the complex II substrate succinate in the presence of ADP (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1E.

claim: In saponin-permeabilized cells, metformin significantly inhibited complex I-dependent respiration at a much lower concentration than that required to inhibit oxygen consumption of intact cells.
source: Interestingly, in saponin-permeabilized cells, metformin significantly inhibited complex I-dependent respiration at a much lower concentration than that required to inhibit oxygen consumption of intact cells, suggesting that transport across the plasma membrane is a barrier to metformin's inhibition of complex I.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing data in Figure 1A (intact cells) and Figure 1C (permeabilized cells).

claim: Transport across the plasma membrane is a barrier to metformin's inhibition of complex I.
source: Interestingly, in saponin-permeabilized cells, metformin significantly inhibited complex I-dependent respiration at a much lower concentration than that required to inhibit oxygen consumption of intact cells, suggesting that transport across the plasma membrane is a barrier to metformin's inhibition of complex I.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that permeabilized cells are more sensitive to metformin than intact cells.

claim: Metformin is known to slowly accumulate in cells in which its uptake is mediated by organic cation transporters (OCTs).
source: Metformin is known to slowly accumulate in cells in which its uptake is mediated by organic cation transporters (OCTs) (Emami Riedmaier et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Expression of OCT1 protein did not change with the presence of NDI1.
source: Expression of OCT1 protein did not change with the presence of NDI1 (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 1F.

claim: Metformin did not induce cell death in Control-HCT 116 p53−/− or NDI1-HCT 116 p53−/− cells in the presence of glucose.
source: Metformin did not induce cell death in Control-HCT 116 p53−/− or NDI1-HCT 116 p53−/− cells in the presence of glucose (Figure 2A,B)
evidence: This is supported by cell viability data in Figure 2A,B.

claim: In the absence of glucose, metformin induced cell death in Control-HCT 116 p53−/− but not in NDI1-HCT 116 p53−/− cells.
source: however, in the absence of glucose, metformin induced cell death in Control-HCT 116 p53−/− but not in NDI1-HCT 116 p53−/− cells (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is supported by cell viability data in Figure 2C,D.

claim: Metformin diminished cell proliferation in Control-HCT 116 p53−/− cells but not in NDI1-HCT 116 p53−/− cells in media containing glucose.
source: Metformin diminished cell proliferation in Control-HCT 116 p53−/− cells but not in NDI1-HCT 116 p53−/− cells in media containing glucose (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: This is supported by cell proliferation data in Figure 2E,F.

claim: The metformin-dependent inhibition of complex I decreases cell proliferation in the presence of glucose and increases cell death under glucose deprivation.
source: These results indicate that the metformin-dependent inhibition of complex I decreases cell proliferation in the presence of glucose and increases cell death under glucose deprivation.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the cell proliferation and viability data in Figure 2.

claim: The inhibitory effects of metformin were not specific to HCT116 p53−/− cells.
source: These inhibitory effects of metformin were not specific to HCT116 p53−/− cells as metformin inhibited oxygen consumption and cellular proliferation of Control-HCT 116 p53+/+ cells and Control-A549 human lung cancer cells but not NDI1-HCT 116 p53+/+ or NDI1-A549 cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and 2.

claim: Metformin inhibited oxygen consumption and cellular proliferation of Control-HCT 116 p53+/+ cells and Control-A549 human lung cancer cells but not NDI1-HCT 116 p53+/+ or NDI1-A549 cells.
source: These inhibitory effects of metformin were not specific to HCT116 p53−/− cells as metformin inhibited oxygen consumption and cellular proliferation of Control-HCT 116 p53+/+ cells and Control-A549 human lung cancer cells but not NDI1-HCT 116 p53+/+ or NDI1-A549 cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and 2.

claim: The anti-proliferative and cell death promoting effects of metformin require mitochondrial complex I inhibition.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that the anti-proliferative and cell death promoting effects of metformin require mitochondrial complex I inhibition.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the genetic rescue experiments with NDI1 across multiple cell lines.

claim: Phenformin is a more lipophilic biguanide.
source: We also examined whether phenformin, a more lipophilic biguanide, also exert its anti-proliferative effects on cancer cells through inhibition of complex I.
evidence: This is stated as a known property of phenformin.

claim: Phenformin inhibited oxygen consumption in Control-HCT 116 p53−/− cells at 100-fold lower concentration compared to metformin.
source: Phenformin inhibited oxygen consumption in Control-HCT 116 p53−/− cells and saponin-permeabilized Control HCT 116 p53−/− cells at 100-fold lower concentration compared to metformin (Figure 3A,C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3A,C.

claim: Expression of NDI1 rescued the phenformin-mediated decrease in oxygen consumption.
source: Expression of NDI1 rescued the phenformin-mediated decrease in oxygen consumption (Figure 3B,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3B,D.

claim: Phenformin diminished cell proliferation in the control but not NDI1 expressing HCT116 p53−/− cells.
source: Phenformin diminished cell proliferation in the control but not NDI1 expressing HCT116 p53−/− cells (Figure 3E,F)
evidence: This is supported by cell proliferation data in Figure 3E,F.

claim: Phenformin did not induce cell death in media containing glucose, similar to metformin.
source: and did not induce cell death in media containing glucose, similar to metformin (Figure 3G,H).
evidence: This is supported by cell viability data in Figure 3G,H.

claim: Phenformin exerts its biological effects through inhibition of mitochondrial complex I.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that phenformin also exerts its biological effects through inhibition of mitochondrial complex I.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the genetic rescue experiments with NDI1 for phenformin.

claim: Metformin inhibited proliferation of wild-type Control-CCL16 hamster fibroblasts but not that of B2-CCL16 cells or of B2-CCL16 cells reconstituted with NDI1 (NDI1-CCL16).
source: Metformin inhibited proliferation of wild-type Control-CCL16 hamster fibroblasts but not that of B2-CCL16 cells or of B2-CCL16 cells reconstituted with NDI1 (NDI1-CCL16).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Metformin and phenformin inhibited cellular oxygen consumption in wild-type CCL16 but not in CCL16-NDI1 cells.
source: Metformin and phenformin inhibited cellular oxygen consumption in wild-type CCL16 but not in CCL16-NDI1 cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and 2.

claim: When CCL16 cells were cultured in galactose-substituted media, both metformin and phenformin induced cell death only in wild-type CCL16 cells.
source: When these cells were cultured in galactose-substituted media, both metformin and phenformin induced cell death only in wild-type CCL16 cells.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: Survival of NDI1-CCL16 cells was not affected by metformin or phenformin.
source: Survival of NDI1-CCL16 cells was not affected by metformin or phenformin (Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: The anti-proliferative effects of metformin and phenformin require mitochondrial complex I inhibition.
source: Taken together, these results confirm that the anti-proliferative effects of metformin and phenformin require mitochondrial complex I inhibition.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from experiments with CCL16 cells lacking functional complex I.

claim: The positive charge of metformin has been proposed to account for it is accumulation within the matrix of mitochondria that exhibit a robust inner mitochondria membrane potential.
source: The positive charge of metformin has been proposed to account for it is accumulation within the matrix of mitochondria that exhibit a robust inner mitochondria membrane potential (Owen et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Metformin inhibited ADP but not CCCP stimulated oxygen consumption indicating that the metformin-mediated inhibition of mitochondrial complex I required polarized mitochondria.
source: Metformin inhibited ADP but not CCCP stimulated oxygen consumption indicating that the metformin-mediated inhibition of mitochondrial complex I required polarized mitochondria (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 4A,B.

claim: Rotenone, an irreversible inhibitor of complex I, does not require polarized mitochondria to inhibit mitochondrial oxygen consumption.
source: Rotenone, an irreversible inhibitor of complex I, does not require polarized mitochondria to inhibit mitochondrial oxygen consumption (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 4C,D.

claim: Metformin treatment did not reduce the mitochondrial inner membrane potential measured using TMRE fluorescent dye in Control and NDI1 HCT116 p53−/− cells.
source: However, we did not observe a reduction in the mitochondrial inner membrane potential measured using TMRE fluorescent dye in Control and NDI1 HCT116 p53−/− cells after metformin treatment (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: This is supported by TMRE fluorescence data in Figure 4E,F.

claim: When electron transport function is inhibited, the ATP synthase can function in reverse such that it uses ATP generated by glycolysis to pump protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane, maintaining membrane potential.
source: When electron transport function is inhibited, the ATP synthase can function in reverse such that it uses ATP generated by glycolysis to pump protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane, maintaining membrane potential (Appleby et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The ATP synthase inhibitor, Oligomycin A, diminished TMRE fluorescence in Control-HCT 116 p53−/− cells treated with metformin.
source: The ATP synthase inhibitor, Oligomycin A, diminished TMRE fluorescence in Control-HCT 116 p53−/− cells treated with metformin suggesting that in the presence of metformin, intact cells maintain their mitochondrial membrane potential by reversal of the ATP synthase (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by TMRE fluorescence data in Figure 4E.

claim: In the presence of metformin, intact cells maintain their mitochondrial membrane potential by reversal of the ATP synthase.
source: The ATP synthase inhibitor, Oligomycin A, diminished TMRE fluorescence in Control-HCT 116 p53−/− cells treated with metformin suggesting that in the presence of metformin, intact cells maintain their mitochondrial membrane potential by reversal of the ATP synthase (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Oligomycin A reduces membrane potential in metformin-treated cells.

claim: Rotenone irreversibly inhibits complex I, which contributes to its high toxicity in vivo.
source: Rotenone irreversibly inhibits complex I, which contributes to its high toxicity in vivo.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about rotenone.

claim: Metformin reversibly inhibits mitochondrial complex I.
source: Metformin inhibited ADP, but not CCCP-stimulated oxygen consumption (Figure 5A,B). As metformin accumulation requires mitochondrial membrane polarization (Figure 4A,B), these results indicate that metformin reversibly inhibits mitochondrial complex I.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that CCCP can restore respiration after metformin treatment.

claim: Mitochondrial complexes I and III produce superoxide into the mitochondrial matrix, where it is converted quickly to H2O2 by SOD2.
source: Mitochondrial complexes I and III produce superoxide into the mitochondrial matrix, where it is converted quickly to H2O2 by SOD2 (Brand, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Mitochondrial complex III also generates superoxide into the mitochondrial intermembrane space where it escapes through VDACs to cytosol and is converted into H2O2 by SOD1.
source: Mitochondrial complex III also generates superoxide into the mitochondrial intermembrane space where it escapes through VDACs to cytosol and is converted into H2O2 by SOD1 (Han et al., 2003; Muller et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Rotenone and antimycin increased the release of H2O2 from mitochondria isolated from Control-HCT 116 p53−/− cells.
source: Consistent with previous reports, rotenone and antimycin increased the release of H2O2 from mitochondria isolated from Control-HCT 116 p53−/− cells (Figure 6A,B; St-Pierre et al., 2002; Muller et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by Amplex Red data in Figure 6A,B and citations to prior research.

claim: Metformin did not substantially increase H2O2 release from isolated mitochondria.
source: In contrast, metformin did not substantially increase H2O2 release, suggesting that metformin and rotenone act on different sites of complex I (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by Amplex Red data in Figure 6A.

claim: Metformin and rotenone act on different sites of complex I.
source: In contrast, metformin did not substantially increase H2O2 release, suggesting that metformin and rotenone act on different sites of complex I (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is inferred from the different effects on H2O2 production.

claim: When mitochondria were isolated from NDI1–HCT 116 p53−/− cells, only antimycin lead to a significant increase in H2O2 release.
source: When mitochondria were isolated from NDI1–HCT 116 p53−/− cells, only antimycin lead to a significant increase in H2O2 release (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by Amplex Red data in Figure 6B.

claim: Metformin does not substantially increase H2O2 production in isolated liver mitochondria.
source: Previous reports have shown that metformin does not substantially increase H2O2 production in isolated liver mitochondria and that metformin diminishes mitochondrial H2O2 production in response to paraquat, which induces mitochondrial ROS production (Batandier et al., 2006; Algire et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Metformin diminishes mitochondrial H2O2 production in response to paraquat, which induces mitochondrial ROS production.
source: Previous reports have shown that metformin does not substantially increase H2O2 production in isolated liver mitochondria and that metformin diminishes mitochondrial H2O2 production in response to paraquat, which induces mitochondrial ROS production (Batandier et al., 2006; Algire et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: One biological consequence of mitochondrial-generated H2O2 is hypoxic stabilization of the hypoxia-inducible factors (HIFs).
source: One biological consequence of mitochondrial-generated H2O2 is hypoxic stabilization of the hypoxia-inducible factors (HIFs) (Chandel et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: HIFs are involved in metabolic adaptation of tumor cells to hypoxia.
source: HIFs are involved in metabolic adaptation of tumor cells to hypoxia (Semenza, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Metformin reduced hypoxic stabilization of HIF-1α in Control-HCT 116 p53−/− but not in NDI1-HCT 116 p53−/−.
source: Metformin reduced hypoxic stabilization of HIF-1α in Control-HCT 116 p53−/− but not in NDI1-HCT 116 p53−/− (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 6C,D.

claim: Metformin did not decrease deferoxamine (DFO) stabilization of HIF-1α protein.
source: Metformin did not decrease deferoxamine (DFO) stabilization of HIF-1α protein.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 6C.

claim: DFO is an iron chelator known to directly stabilize HIF-1α protein independent of upstream signaling events.
source: DFO is an iron chelator known to directly stabilize HIF-1α protein independent of upstream signaling events.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about DFO.

claim: Metformin significantly diminished hypoxic activation of HIF-dependent target genes, vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), and carbonic anhydrase 9 (CA9) in Control-HCT 116 p53−/− but not in NDI1-HCT 116 p53−/−.
source: Metformin also significantly diminished hypoxic activation of HIF-dependent target genes, vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), and carbonic anhydrase 9 (CA9) in Control-HCT 116 p53−/− but not in NDI1-HCT 116 p53−/− (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data in Figure 6E.

claim: Metformin is an effective agent to reduce hypoxic activation of HIF-1.
source: Thus, metformin is an effective agent to reduce hypoxic activation of HIF-1.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the HIF-1α protein and target gene expression data.

claim: Control-HCT 116 p53−/− cells subcutaneously injected into the left flank of nude mice rapidly grew in vivo.
source: Control-HCT 116 p53−/− cells subcutaneously injected into the left flank of nude mice rapidly grew in vivo, while tumors from mice fed metformin through drinking water ad libitum starting 4 days post-implantation exhibited a marked reduction in growth (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: This is supported by tumor growth data in Figure 7A,B.

claim: Tumors from mice fed metformin through drinking water ad libitum starting 4 days post-implantation exhibited a marked reduction in growth.
source: Control-HCT 116 p53−/− cells subcutaneously injected into the left flank of nude mice rapidly grew in vivo, while tumors from mice fed metformin through drinking water ad libitum starting 4 days post-implantation exhibited a marked reduction in growth (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: This is supported by tumor growth data in Figure 7A,B.

claim: NDI1-HCT 116 p53−/− xenograft growth was resistant to metformin therapy.
source: NDI1-HCT 116 p53−/− xenograft growth was resistant to metformin therapy (Figure 7A,B), suggesting that the metformin carries out its tumor inhibitory effects in a cancer cell autonomous manner through inhibition of mitochondrial complex I.
evidence: This is supported by tumor growth data in Figure 7A,B.

claim: The consumption of water containing metformin was similar between control and NDI1 tumor barring mice.
source: Importantly, the consumption of water containing metformin was similar between control and NDI1 tumor barring mice (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by water consumption data in Figure 7C.

claim: Transcripts for the HIF target genes CA9 and VEGF were diminished in control tumors treated with metformin but not in NDI1 expressing tumors.
source: Transcripts for the HIF target genes CA9 and VEGF were diminished in control tumors treated with metformin but not in NDI1 expressing tumors (Figure 7D,E).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data in Figure 7D,E.

claim: The blood glucose, plasma lactate, insulin, and IGF-1 level displayed no differences between the metformin-treated animals and control animals at the end of the study.
source: The blood glucose, plasma lactate, insulin, and IGF-1 level displayed no differences between the metformin-treated animals and control animals at the end of the study (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), consistent with previous reports (Tomimoto et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and citation to prior research.

claim: Metformin acts as a complex I inhibitor in vitro and in vivo to inhibit tumorigenesis.
source: In the present study, we genetically demonstrate that metformin acts as a complex I inhibitor in vitro and in vivo to inhibit tumorigenesis.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from all the experimental data.

claim: Mitochondrial metabolism is essential for cancer proliferation.
source: Our current findings bolster our previous findings highlighting the importance of mitochondrial metabolism as essential for cancer proliferation (Weinberg et al., 2010; Sullivan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research from the authors.

claim: Phenformin exerts its anti-tumor effects by inhibiting complex I.
source: Our results are consistent with a recent report demonstrating another biguanide phenformin exerts its anti-tumor effects by inhibiting complex I (Birsoy et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent report.

claim: Phenformin has been discontinued because of frequent occurrence of lactic acidosis.
source: However, unlike metformin, phenformin has been discontinued because of frequent occurrence of lactic acidosis (Bailey and Turner, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Cancer cells that express insulin receptors might be affected by metformin's inhibition on hepatic gluconeogenesis to reduce circulating insulin levels.
source: Specifically, cancer cells that express insulin receptors might be affected by metformin's inhibition on hepatic gluconeogenesis to reduce circulating insulin levels (Goodwin et al., 2012).
evidence: This is presented as a possibility and supported by citation.

claim: The levels of metformin within cells is regulated by a balance between uptake mechanisms, which are dependent on expression of organic cation transporters (OCT 1, 2, and 3), and expulsion mechanisms, which are dependent on expression on multidrug and toxin extrusion proteins (MATE1 and MATE 2).
source: The levels of metformin within cells is regulated by a balance between uptake mechanisms, which are dependent on expression of organic cation transporters (OCT 1, 2, and 3), and expulsion mechanisms, which are dependent on expression on multidrug and toxin extrusion proteins (MATE1 and MATE 2) (Emami Riedmaier et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Cancer cells are likely to have a wide range in expression of uptake and extrusion proteins allowing for metformin accumulation.
source: Cancer cells are likely to have a wide range in expression of uptake and extrusion proteins allowing for metformin accumulation.
evidence: This is stated as a likely scenario based on known biology.

claim: The uptake of metformin in mitochondria is also dependent on mitochondrial membrane potential.
source: The uptake of metformin in mitochondria is also dependent on mitochondrial membrane potential.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data in Figure 4.

claim: Metformin exists as a cation at physiological pH.
source: Metformin exists as a cation at physiological pH and thus its accumulation within mitochondria is predicted to increase as a function of the mitochondrial membrane potential.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about metformin chemistry.

claim: Metformin's accumulation within mitochondria is predicted to increase as a function of the mitochondrial membrane potential.
source: Metformin exists as a cation at physiological pH and thus its accumulation within mitochondria is predicted to increase as a function of the mitochondrial membrane potential.
evidence: This is inferred from the cationic nature of metformin and the negative charge inside mitochondria.

claim: The inhibition of electron transport at complex I by metformin should reduce the mitochondrial membrane potential as proton pumping is linked to electron transport.
source: The inhibition of electron transport at complex I by metformin should reduce the mitochondrial membrane potential as proton pumping is linked to electron transport.
evidence: This is inferred from basic mitochondrial biology.

claim: Metformin-treated cells maintain their mitochondrial membrane potential in part due to the reversal of the ATP synthase.
source: However, we observed that metformin-treated cells maintain their mitochondrial membrane potential in part due to the reversal of the ATP synthase thus allowing accumulation of metformin in the mitochondrial matrix (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by the oligomycin data in Figure 4E.

claim: Cells with compromised ETC can sustain mitochondrial membrane potential through reversal of ATP synthase.
source: It is well known that cells with compromised ETC can sustain mitochondrial membrane potential through this mechanism (Appleby et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Metformin will inhibit mitochondrial complex I and decrease tumorigenesis in cancer cells that have transporters across the plasma membrane, as well as a robust inner mitochondrial membrane potential.
source: Collectively, our results indicate that will inhibit mitochondrial complex I and decrease tumorigenesis in cancer cells that have transporters across the plasma membrane, as well as a robust inner mitochondrial membrane potential to allow metformin to reach the mitochondrial matrix.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: Metformin's efficacy as an anti-cancer agent may be dependent on the tumor expression of OCTs.
source: It will be of interest to observe whether metformin's efficacy as an anti-cancer agent is dependent on the tumor expression of OCTs.
evidence: This is presented as a hypothesis for future investigation.

claim: Metformin's inhibition on mitochondrial complex I is distinct from the classical complex I inhibitor rotenone.
source: Our study also reveals that metformin's inhibition on mitochondrial complex I is distinct from the classical complex I inhibitor rotenone.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data comparing metformin and rotenone effects.

claim: Metformin requires a robust mitochondrial membrane potential to accumulate in the mitochondrial matrix and reversibly inhibits complex I.
source: Metformin requires a robust mitochondrial membrane potential to accumulate in the mitochondrial matrix and reversibly inhibits complex I.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Rotenone is an irreversible inhibitor of complex I that does not require mitochondrial membrane potential.
source: By contrast, rotenone is an irreversible inhibitor of complex I that does not require mitochondrial membrane potential.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data in Figure 4C,D.

claim: Rotenone accumulation is not dependent on specific transporters expressed in the plasma membrane and readily accumulates in all cells and thus is highly toxic.
source: Rotenone accumulation is not dependent on specific transporters expressed in the plasma membrane and readily accumulates in all cells and thus is highly toxic.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about rotenone.

claim: Metformin does not promote generation of ROS from complex I, while rotenone stimulates ROS production from complex I.
source: Furthermore, metformin does not promote generation of ROS from complex I, while rotenone stimulates ROS production from complex I (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by the Amplex Red data in Figure 6A.

claim: The flavin site within Complex I produces ROS.
source: The flavin site within Complex I produces ROS and previous studies indicate that rotenone inhibits complex I downstream of the flavin site, stimulating ROS generation (Pryde and Hirst, 2011; St-Pierre et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Rotenone inhibits complex I downstream of the flavin site, stimulating ROS generation.
source: The flavin site within Complex I produces ROS and previous studies indicate that rotenone inhibits complex I downstream of the flavin site, stimulating ROS generation (Pryde and Hirst, 2011; St-Pierre et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Metformin acts upstream of the flavin site, inhibiting complex I activity while also inhibiting ROS generation.
source: It is likely that metformin acts upstream of this site, inhibiting complex I activity while also inhibiting ROS generation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that metformin does not increase ROS production.

claim: Mitochondrial complex III also produces ROS.
source: Mitochondrial complex III also produces ROS (Muller et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Metformin by inhibiting the complex I would limit electron flow to complex III thereby reducing ROS generation from complex III.
source: Therefore, metformin by inhibiting the complex I would limit electron flow to complex III thereby reducing ROS generation from complex III.
evidence: This is inferred from the mechanism of electron transport chain function.

claim: A consequence of mitochondrial complex III ROS generation is the hypoxic activation of HIF-1.
source: A consequence of mitochondrial complex III ROS generation is the hypoxic activation of HIF-1 (Bell et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Metformin might be an effective treatment for diseases associated with hyperactivation of HIF such as pulmonary hypertension.
source: Beyond cancer, metformin might be an effective treatment for diseases associated with hyperactivation of HIF such as pulmonary hypertension (Shimoda and Semenza, 2011).
evidence: This is presented as a speculation based on the HIF inhibition data, with citation support.

claim: The concentration of metformin administered to mice in this report is predicted to achieve plasma concentrations of metformin similar to those in humans receiving metformin therapy.
source: The concentration of metformin we administered to mice in this report is predicted to achieve plasma concentrations of metformin similar to those in humans receiving metformin therapy.
evidence: This is supported by the dose conversion calculations and citations provided in the discussion.

claim: Metformin was administered to drinking water at a concentration of 1.25 mg/ml, approximately 250 mg/kg.
source: In our study, metformin was administered to drinking water at a concentration of 1.25 mg/ml, approximately 250 mg/kg.
evidence: This is stated as the experimental dosing regimen.

claim: The human equivalent dose of 250 mg/kg metformin in mice is 20.27 mg/kg or 1418 mg for a 70 kg adult.
source: Conversion of doses from mice to human is achieved using a formula based on body surface area normalization (Reagan-Shaw et al., 2008). The human equivalent dose of 250 mg/kg metformin in mice is 20.27 mg/kg or 1418 mg for a 70 kg adult.
evidence: This is calculated using a cited formula for dose conversion.

claim: Patients typically receive 500–2500 mg metformin per day.
source: Patients typically receive 500–2500 mg metformin per day (Scarpello and Howlett, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to clinical literature.

claim: In patients receiving metformin therapy, plasma levels range between 0.5–2 µg/ml; approximately 4 µM–15 µM.
source: In these patients receiving metformin therapy, plasma levels range between 0.5–2 µg/ml; approximately 4 µM–15 µM (Graham et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to clinical literature.

claim: Mice receiving drinking water containing 1–5 mg/ml of metformin have a plasma steady-state metformin concentration of 0.45–1.7 µg/ml.
source: Previous studies have shown that mice receiving drinking water containing 1–5 mg/ml of metformin have a plasma steady-state metformin concentration of 0.45–1.7 µg/ml (Memmott et al., 2010), indicating that our metformin dosage falls within a clinically relevant range.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The metformin dosage used in this study falls within a clinically relevant range.
source: Previous studies have shown that mice receiving drinking water containing 1–5 mg/ml of metformin have a plasma steady-state metformin concentration of 0.45–1.7 µg/ml (Memmott et al., 2010), indicating that our metformin dosage falls within a clinically relevant range.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the mouse dosing to human plasma levels.

claim: Metformin concentrations (250–1000 µM) used for in vitro experiments in this report are in the range utilized by investigators in the diabetes field to examine the effects of metformin on primary murine and human hepatocytes.
source: Metformin concentrations (250–1000 µM) used for in vitro experiments in this report are in the range utilized by investigators in the diabetes field to examine the effects of metformin on primary murine and human hepatocytes (Foretz et al., 2010; Stephenne et al., 2011; Miller et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The metformin concentrations required to induce biological effects in vitro are a magnitude of order higher than plasma level concentrations of metformin in vivo.
source: A perplexing observation revealed in our study and previous studies is that the metformin concentrations required to induce biological effects in vitro are a magnitude of order higher than plasma level concentrations of metformin in vivo.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the current and prior studies.

claim: A likely cause for the difference between in vitro and in vivo metformin concentrations is the accumulation of metformin in liver or tumors to local concentrations that are much higher than in the circulating plasma.
source: A likely cause for this difference is the accumulation of metformin in liver or tumors to local concentrations that are much higher than in the circulating plasma.
evidence: This is presented as a likely explanation for the concentration discrepancy.

claim: The gut has been shown to accumulate metformin in the mM range.
source: Indeed, the gut has been shown to accumulate metformin in the mM range (Bailey et al., 2008; Proctor et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Metformin reversibly inhibits mitochondrial complex I within cancer cells to reduce tumorigenesis.
source: In summary, our results indicate that metformin reversibly inhibits mitochondrial complex I within cancer cells to reduce tumorigenesis.
evidence: This is the main conclusion summarizing the study findings.

claim: Metformin inhibits tumorigenesis through multiple mechanisms including the induction of cancer cell death in conditions, when glucose is limited.
source: Metformin inhibits tumorigenesis through multiple mechanisms including the induction of cancer cell death in conditions, when glucose is limited and through inhibition of mitochondrial ROS-dependent signaling pathways that promote tumorigenesis (i.e., HIF).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on cell death and HIF inhibition.

claim: Metformin inhibits tumorigenesis through inhibition of mitochondrial ROS-dependent signaling pathways that promote tumorigenesis (i.e., HIF).
source: Metformin inhibits tumorigenesis through multiple mechanisms including the induction of cancer cell death in conditions, when glucose is limited and through inhibition of mitochondrial ROS-dependent signaling pathways that promote tumorigenesis (i.e., HIF).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the HIF inhibition data.

claim: Metformin would be most effective in low glucose and oxygen conditions.
source: These results indicate that metformin would be most effective in low glucose and oxygen conditions.
evidence: This is inferred from the mechanisms of action identified in the study.

claim: Metformin treatment might provide a useful adjunct to therapies that limit glucose uptake (e.g., PI3K inhibitors) or drive tumors to low glucose and oxygen levels (e.g., anti-angiogenic inhibitors).
source: It will be of interest to determine whether metformin treatment might provide a useful adjunct to therapies that limit glucose uptake (e.g., PI3K inhibitors) or drive tumors to low glucose and oxygen levels (e.g., anti-angiogenic inhibitors).
evidence: This is presented as a speculation for future therapeutic strategies.

claim: NDI1-HCT 116 p53−/− cells demonstrated a slight, non-significant elevation in basal cellular oxygen consumption compared to control cells.
source: NDI1-HCT 116 p53−/− cells demonstrated a slight, non-significant elevation in basal cellular oxygen consumption compared to control cells and were completely resistant to the effects of metformin on cellular oxygen consumption (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Control-A549 cells subcutaneously injected into the left flank of nude mice rapidly grew in vivo.
source: Control-A549 cells subcutaneously injected into the left flank of nude mice rapidly grew in vivo, while tumors from mice fed metformin through drinking water ad libitum starting 2 weeks prior to tumor induction exhibited a marked reduction in growth over 45 days (Figure 7—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is supported by tumor growth data in Figure 7—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Tumors from mice fed metformin through drinking water ad libitum starting 2 weeks prior to tumor induction exhibited a marked reduction in growth over 45 days.
source: Control-A549 cells subcutaneously injected into the left flank of nude mice rapidly grew in vivo, while tumors from mice fed metformin through drinking water ad libitum starting 2 weeks prior to tumor induction exhibited a marked reduction in growth over 45 days (Figure 7—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is supported by tumor growth data in Figure 7—figure supplement 3B.

claim: NDI1-NDUFS3-A549 xenografts were completely resistant to metformin therapy.
source: By contrast, NDI1-NDUFS3-A549 xenografts were completely resistant to metformin therapy, suggesting that metformin carries out its tumor inhibitory effects in a cell autonomous manner through inhibition of mitochondrial complex I in these cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is supported by tumor growth data in Figure 7—figure supplement 3C.

claim: NDI1-NDUFS3-A549 xenografts grew slower than control xenografts in untreated mice.
source: NDI1-NDUFS3-A549 xenografts grew slower than control xenografts in untreated mice.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the xenograft experiments.
